indicators.name: Blood pressure
indicators.todo: Verify the low-pressure (hypotension) cut-offs; AHA categories cover the high side only.
indicators.whyItMatters: Without gravity, body fluids shift towards your head and your heart and blood vessels adapt. Stress and poor sleep can also push pressure up.

plainMeaning.nominal: Your blood pressure is in the normal range.
plainMeaning.watch: A little above (or below) your normal. Rest, then measure again.
plainMeaning.act: Clearly outside the safe range. Follow the steps now and watch the escalation rule.
plainMeaning.stale: Not measured recently. Take a reading to update.

howToSteps.text: Sit still for 5 minutes with your feet anchored and your back supported.
Wrap the cuff around your bare upper arm, about 2 cm above the elbow crease.
Rest your arm at heart height. Don't talk or move.
Press start and wait while the cuff inflates and slowly releases.
Read both numbers: top (systolic) and bottom (diastolic).

recoveryActions.text: Sit and rest for 10 minutes, then measure again.
Keep salt low today and drink water as planned.
Protect a full sleep period tonight.
Do your scheduled aerobic exercise; avoid heavy lifting until the next reading.

redFlags: Very bad headache or blurred vision
Weak or numb on one side, or trouble speaking
escalationRule.onboard: Tell the Crew Medical Officer (CMO). Rest, re-measure every 4 h, and follow the on-board medical guide: high blood pressure.
escalationRule.earth: Send a Ground Link report so the flight surgeon has the record. A reply can take weeks, so never wait for it before acting.

glossary.Systolic: The top number: pressure while your heart beats.
glossary.Diastolic: The bottom number: pressure while your heart rests between beats.
glossary.mmHg: Millimetres of mercury, the unit used for blood pressure.
glossary.CMO: Crew Medical Officer: the crewmate trained in first aid and the on-board medical kit.

sources.title: American Heart Association: Understanding blood pressure readings
NASA Human Research Program: Hazards of human spaceflight
sources.usedFor: Fluid shift and cardiovascular adaptation context

indicators.name: Heart rate and HRV
indicators.todo: HRV cut-offs are demo assumptions; HRV is mostly judged against your own baseline.
indicators.whyItMatters: Resting heart rate and heart-rate variability (HRV) show how hard your heart is working and how well you are recovering from stress and poor sleep.

plainMeaning.nominal: Your heart is working at its usual pace and recovering well.
plainMeaning.watch: Your heart is working harder than usual, or recovering less. Rest and measure again.
plainMeaning.act: Your heart rate is clearly outside the safe range. Follow the steps now.
plainMeaning.stale: Not measured recently. Take a reading to update.

howToSteps.text: Put on the Bio-Monitor shirt and check that the sensors touch your skin.
Lie or sit still and breathe normally for 1 minute.
Press start and stay still while the ECG trace records.
Check the trace looks steady, then save the reading.

recoveryActions.text: Rest for 15 minutes; slow breathing, 6 breaths per minute.
Drink water and skip caffeine for the rest of the day.
Aim for a full 8-hour sleep period tonight.
Tell a crewmate how you feel.

redFlags: Heart racing at rest for more than 10 minutes
escalationRule.onboard: Tell the CMO. Lie down, record an ECG with the Bio-Monitor every 2 h, and follow the on-board medical guide: heart rhythm.
escalationRule.earth: Send a Ground Link report so the flight surgeon has the record. A reply can take weeks, so never wait for it before acting.

glossary.HRV: Heart-rate variability: small changes in time between beats. Higher usually means better recovery.
glossary.ECG: Electrocardiogram: a recording of your heart's electrical activity.
glossary.CMO: Crew Medical Officer: the crewmate trained in first aid and the on-board medical kit.

sources.title: American Heart Association: Target heart rates
sources.usedFor: Resting heart rate normal range (60–100 bpm; widened for trained crew)

sources.title: Shaffer & Ginsberg (2017) An overview of heart rate variability metrics and norms, Front. Public Health

indicators.name: Blood oxygen (SpO₂)
indicators.whyItMatters: Shows how much oxygen your blood carries. Cabin air problems or a chest infection can lower it.

plainMeaning.nominal: Your blood is carrying a normal amount of oxygen.
plainMeaning.watch: Slightly low. Check the cabin air reading and measure again.
plainMeaning.act: Low oxygen. Follow the steps now.
plainMeaning.stale: Not measured recently. Take a reading to update.

howToSteps.text: Warm your hands and remove any nail coating from the test finger.
Clip the oximeter on your index finger, nail side up.
Rest your hand still at chest height for 30 seconds.
Read the steady number once the pulse wave is regular.

recoveryActions.text: Check the cabin O₂/CO₂ display and move to a well-ventilated module.
Sit upright and take slow, deep breaths for 5 minutes, then re-measure.
Ask a crewmate to check their own reading to rule out a cabin issue.

escalationRule.onboard: Check the cabin air display first. If the air is fine, tell the CMO and sit upright; the CMO decides on oxygen using the on-board guide.
escalationRule.earth: Send a Ground Link report so the flight surgeon has the record. A reply can take weeks, so never wait for it before acting.

glossary.SpO₂: Peripheral oxygen saturation: the share of your red blood cells carrying oxygen.
glossary.CMO: Crew Medical Officer: the crewmate trained in first aid and the on-board medical kit.

indicators.name: Body temperature
indicators.whyItMatters: Your immune system changes in space. A fever can be the first sign of an infection.

plainMeaning.watch: Slightly raised (or low). Measure again in a few hours.
plainMeaning.act: Fever (or too cold). Follow the steps now.
plainMeaning.stale: Not measured recently. Take a reading to update.

howToSteps.text: Wear the Bio-Monitor shirt for at least 10 minutes before reading.
Avoid exercise or hot drinks for 20 minutes.
Press start and stay still for 30 seconds.

recoveryActions.text: Rest, drink fluids and note any other symptoms (cough, sore throat, rash).
Limit close contact with crewmates until the next reading.
Take an extra rest period if the schedule allows.

redFlags: A rash that does not fade when you press a glass on it
escalationRule.onboard: Tell the CMO. Rest in your own crew quarters and drink fluids. The CMO decides on any treatment using the on-board guide.
escalationRule.earth: Send a Ground Link report so the flight surgeon has the record. A reply can take weeks, so never wait for it before acting.

glossary.Fever: A body temperature of 38.0 °C or higher.
glossary.CMO: Crew Medical Officer: the crewmate trained in first aid and the on-board medical kit.

indicators.name: Sleep
indicators.todo: Watch at < 6 h is a demo assumption (AASM recommends ≥ 7 h; < 7 h on every short night flagged steady crew too often). Quality cut-offs are demo assumptions.
indicators.whyItMatters: Noise, light, workload and no day–night cycle make sleep hard in space. Poor sleep affects mood, focus and your heart.

plainMeaning.watch: Less sleep than you need. Protect tonight's sleep period.
plainMeaning.act: Severe lack of sleep. Follow the recovery plan today.
plainMeaning.stale: No sleep log for last night. Add one to update.

howToSteps.text: Wear the actigraphy watch through your sleep period.
When you wake, check the hours it logged.
Rate how rested you feel from 1 to 10.

recoveryActions.text: Lights out at 22:00; no screens for 1 h before.
20 minutes of morning exercise, not in the 3 h before sleep.
No caffeine after 14:00.
Crew check-in: talk with a crewmate today.

escalationRule.onboard: Tell the CMO and the commander. Do no safety-critical tasks (EVA, docking, piloting) until you have slept; the schedule is changed on board.
escalationRule.earth: Send a Ground Link report so the flight surgeon has the record. A reply can take weeks, so never wait for it before acting.

glossary.CMO: Crew Medical Officer: the crewmate trained in first aid and the on-board medical kit.

sources.title: Watson et al. (2015) Recommended amount of sleep for a healthy adult (AASM/SRS), J Clin Sleep Med
NASA Human Research Program: Hazards of human spaceflight

indicators.name: Mood, stress and reaction time
indicators.todo: Replace with validated scales (e.g. NASA Cognition battery PVT norms) before any real use.
indicators.whyItMatters: Isolation, confinement and being far from home can slowly wear down mood and focus. A quick test catches the change early.

plainMeaning.nominal: Your mood and reaction time are at your usual level.
plainMeaning.watch: Mood is lower or reactions slower than usual. Take a break and talk to someone.
plainMeaning.act: Mood is very low or reactions much slower. Follow the plan and tell the crew.
plainMeaning.stale: No check-in recently. Take the 30-second check.

howToSteps.text: Find a quiet spot and rate your mood from 1 (very low) to 10 (great).
Start the reaction test: tap as soon as the target lights up.
Five targets appear over about 20 seconds. Stay focused.

recoveryActions.text: Crew check-in: share how you feel with a crewmate.
Schedule a private call or message to family when the link allows.
Do 20 minutes of exercise you enjoy.
Keep a regular sleep time tonight.

redFlags: Unable to do your daily tasks
escalationRule.onboard: Tell the commander or CMO today. Use the buddy system (a crewmate checks on you) and the on-board psychological support kit. Never stay alone with these thoughts.
escalationRule.earth: Send a Ground Link report so the flight surgeon has the record. A reply can take weeks, so never wait for it before acting.

glossary.Reaction time: How fast you respond to a target, in milliseconds. Tiredness slows it down.
glossary.CMO: Crew Medical Officer: the crewmate trained in first aid and the on-board medical kit.

sources.title: Basner et al. (2015) Development and validation of the Cognition test battery for spaceflight, Aerosp Med Hum Perform
sources.usedFor: Reaction-time testing as a spaceflight measure

sources.title: NASA Human Research Program: Hazards of human spaceflight

indicators.name: Blood glucose
indicators.whyItMatters: Less movement and changes in diet and hormones in space can change how your body handles sugar.

plainMeaning.watch: A little high (or low). Check what you ate and measure again.
plainMeaning.act: Blood sugar is far from normal. Follow the steps now.
plainMeaning.stale: Not measured recently. Take a reading to update.

howToSteps.text: Measure before breakfast (fasting) and wash and dry your hands.
Insert a test strip and prick the side of your fingertip.
Touch the drop to the strip and wait for the number.
Dispose of the lancet in the sharps container.

recoveryActions.text: If low: eat 15 g of fast sugar (juice pouch), re-measure after 15 minutes.
If high: drink water, choose a low-sugar menu item for the next meal.
Do your scheduled exercise session.

redFlags: Very thirsty and passing a lot of urine
escalationRule.onboard: If low: eat 15 g of fast sugar now and re-measure in 15 minutes. Tell the CMO and follow the on-board medical guide: blood sugar.
escalationRule.earth: Send a Ground Link report so the flight surgeon has the record. A reply can take weeks, so never wait for it before acting.

glossary.Fasting: No food for at least 8 hours.
glossary.CMO: Crew Medical Officer: the crewmate trained in first aid and the on-board medical kit.

sources.title: American Diabetes Association: Standards of Care in Diabetes

indicators.name: Body mass (weight)
indicators.todo: The ±5 % / ±10 % cut-offs follow the clinical rule of thumb for significant unintended weight change; verify the ISS body-mass device name (SLAMMD) before naming it.
indicators.whyItMatters: Without gravity a normal scale doesn't work, so mass is measured by a device that gently pushes you. Losing weight in space often means you are eating too little and losing muscle and bone.

plainMeaning.nominal: Your weight is steady compared with launch day.
plainMeaning.watch: You have lost (or gained) more than 5 % since launch. Eat every planned meal and keep exercising.
plainMeaning.act: More than 10 % change since launch. Follow the plan today and tell the CMO.
plainMeaning.stale: Not measured this week. Take a reading to update.

howToSteps.text: Measure at the same time each week, before breakfast, after using the toilet.
Wear the same light clothing as last time and empty your pockets.
Sit in the device, hold the handles, tuck your legs in and stay relaxed.
Press start. The device gently moves you back and forth and works out your mass.

recoveryActions.text: Eat every planned meal, plus one extra snack a day until your weight is steady.
Drink your full water ration; log what you eat for 3 days.
Keep your resistance exercise (squats, deadlifts on the trainer) every day.
Eat at least one meal a day together with the crew.

redFlags: Lost more than 2 kg in one week without trying
Feeling very weak or dizzy when you move
escalationRule.onboard: Tell the CMO. Add the extra meals from the food reserve, log everything you eat, and follow the on-board medical guide: weight loss.
escalationRule.earth: Send a Ground Link report so the flight surgeon has the record. A reply can take weeks, so never wait for it before acting.

glossary.Body mass: How much of you there is, in kilograms. In space we measure mass, not weight.
glossary.CMO: Crew Medical Officer: the crewmate trained in first aid and the on-board medical kit.

sources.title: NASA Human Research Program: Hazards of human spaceflight
sources.usedFor: Muscle, bone and nutrition risks in altered gravity

sources.title: MedlinePlus: Weight loss, unintentional
sources.usedFor: Unintended weight change of 5 % or more as a warning sign

indicators.name: Radiation dose
indicators.todo: Career limit (600 mSv) is from NASA-STD-3001; the 50 % / 80 % amber and red fractions are our demo assumption.
indicators.whyItMatters: Outside Earth's magnetic field you get far more radiation. It adds up over the mission and raises long-term cancer risk.

plainMeaning.nominal: Your total dose is well within the mission limit.
plainMeaning.watch: You have used half of your career dose limit. Use shielded areas when you can.
plainMeaning.act: Close to your career limit. Follow shielding steps and contact ground.
plainMeaning.stale: No dosimeter reading recently. Check the dosimeter.

howToSteps.text: Keep the dosimeter clipped to your chest pocket at all times.
Once a day, hold it near the reader to sync.
During a solar storm alert, go to the shielded shelter.

recoveryActions.text: Spend sleep and rest periods in the most shielded module.
Follow solar particle event alerts; shelter when told.
Keep a normal, balanced diet; no supplements without ground advice.

redFlags: Nausea or vomiting after a radiation event
escalationRule.onboard: Go to the shielded shelter during any solar storm alert. Tell the CMO, who logs the dose and follows the on-board radiation guide.
escalationRule.earth: Send a Ground Link report so the flight surgeon has the record. A reply can take weeks, so never wait for it before acting.

glossary.mSv: Millisievert: a unit of radiation dose to the body.
glossary.Career limit: The total dose NASA allows over a whole career.
glossary.CMO: Crew Medical Officer: the crewmate trained in first aid and the on-board medical kit.

sources.title: NASA-STD-3001 Space Flight Human-System Standard, Vol. 1 (career limit 600 mSv)
Zeitlin et al. (2013) Measurements of energetic particle radiation in transit to Mars on the Mars Science Laboratory, Science
sources.usedFor: ~1.8 mSv/day dose rate during Mars cruise (simulation input)

readiness.note: Score = 100 − Σ(weight × penalty), with weights summing to 100. Weights live on each indicator.
